result.summary: Pausanias travels from Corinth toward Argos, describing Cleonæ, the roads through the mountains, and Nemea with its Zeus temple and the legend of Opheltes. He then reaches Mycenæ and starts on early Argive history, recounting Phoroneus and the dispute between Poseidon and Hera.

scenes.title: Cleonæ and its monuments
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Cleonæ, its name, the temple of Athene and the tomb of Eurytus and Cteatus.

scenes.title: Roads and Nemea
scenes.summary: The two roads to Argos lead past the Nemean lion's lair to Nemea, with its temple, the tomb of Opheltes and local names.
scenes.stakes: Opheltes was killed by a dragon while left on the grass by his nurse.

scenes.title: Mycenæ and early Argolis
scenes.summary: Pausanias sights Mycenæ and turns to early Argive history: Inachus, the rivers' judgement for Hera, and Phoroneus gathering men.
scenes.stakes: Poseidon, angered at losing the land, dried up the rivers.

analysis.text: Pausanias ties landmarks to local legends, explaining names and rituals through myth.
Rivers that run dry in summer are explained as Poseidon's punishment, a myth explaining the Argive landscape.

legacy.text: The death of Opheltes was said to be the origin of the Nemean Games.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes the Nemean temple had lost its roof and statue, showing its state in the 2nd century AD.

language_notes.text: Dædalus was the legendary Cretan craftsman; "pupils of Dædalus" marks Scyllis and Dipœnus as early sculptors of wooden images.
Hercules' war against Augeas, king of Elis, whose stables he cleansed; the Elean sons of Molione had fought against him in it.
A stade was a Greek measure of about 600 feet; "Tretus" means "bored" or perforated, perhaps for the road's cut-through character.
Adrastus was the legendary king of Argos who led the Seven against Thebes; the name Adrastea may recall him.
The dispute between Poseidon and Hera over Argos's land is a local myth explaining why the rivers run dry.

context_notes.text: The Nemean lion was a monster killed by Hercules as the first of his labours.
Nemea hosted the Nemean Games, one of the four great Panhellenic festivals, held in honour of Zeus.
Opheltes was the infant whose death, according to legend, led to the founding of the Nemean Games; Lycurgus here is his father.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias lists rival traditions with "some say... others", showing a cautious, report-style voice that avoids choosing between them.
The myth explains a natural fact, the rivers' seasonal dryness, as divine punishment by Poseidon.
